This is by far my favorite strategy game.  

For those of you who are new to Sins it will be a bit of a challenge figuring out how to play the game but trust me put the time in and it pays off. The difficulty of the game can be tweaked to suit anybody's needs, wether your'e looking for a quick 1 on 1 match against an easy opponent or an 8 player free for all against ruthless AI, or compete against real human beings online.  Be warned though, matches can last for hours and hours, this can be a good or bad point depending on your play style.  Visuals are great, so much satisfaction to be had in zooming all the way in on your massive fleets and watching them demolish your rivals empire in flurries of lasers, and explosions.  

Long story short, if your'e into games like Total War, Glactic Civilizations, Supreme Commander then your'e definately going to want to pick this up.  40$ is a little steep though so look for it to go on sale, I was able to pick it up for 8$.

So with over 100 hours, could I recommend this game? Yes, 100% yes. This game is intense fun, solo or with friends and I adore it. The game can be tough and challenging at times and can prove to be a difficult experience to master but once you get its basics down, your empires often grow to be unstoppable. There are 3 factions, TEC (Trader Emergency Coalition) that formed in response to the growing alien assaults on their worlds, the Vasari (Bastards) who are the most brutal and strongest and the Advent (Heavily reminds me of the Covenant from Halo) who while being the weaker in terms of fire power and armour, have the toughest shields and best upgrades and special abilities. Each of these factions have a 'Loyalist' side and a 'Rebel' side which are either more defensive or aggressive which really is up to you which you prefer as they are all balanced.

This game has no single player story to speak of, but in the case of RTS' I rarely care about the story (unless its Command and Conquer), so for those who enjoy a good story this game isn't for you. Gameplay wise, you build huge fleets to combat your enemies above planets to conquer them. Every planet pays taxes and minerals which are used to build ships, with more planets giving you a better economy. The game descibes itself as a 4X game but there is only one way to win, conquest. You can run a diplomatic game where you align yourself with alien factions to survive but a military is still required to survive the long term. The fleets are built up of Cruisers and Frigates as the grunt ships, these will die the most and have specific roles, for example the Cobalt Frigate is your main unit for spam and amassing in huge numbers. Next up is Capital Ships which make up a smaller portion of your fleet and are incredibly expensive, they can also level up which proves to be a great asset in later battles. And finally, Titans, these bad boys take forever to research and build but will often carry you in fights. Losing a Titan is devastating and can crush your fleet.

Other factors such as modding is amazing, my personal mods I switch between is 'Sins of a Galactic Empire' a star wars mod, 'Sins of the Prophets' a fantastically difficult Halo mod and finally 'Star Trek: Armada 3' which is fun despite me not being a Star Trek fan. Online play is decent and I've not seen much toxic attitudes in the community but you never know. And finally DLC, if you have money to spare then they are okay but really I wouldn't waste your money for such things as being able to colonise water planets or adding policies for planets. There are dozens of maps in each format of small, medium and large with you being able to build your own maps which is great.

Overall this game is worth a 9/10, this game is immense fun and proves to be amongst my favourite RTS' of all time and I consistantly return to play. My only issue being the DLC not adding too much but their price kinda makes up to this and the fact that the game does lag a slight bit more with huge space battles, one example of this is when playing with some friends our 6 massive fleets met above an wormhole and the game began to chug due to the large amounts of fighting going on, and the odd clipping issues (bombers flying through planets) does ruin it. Overall there is hardly anything wrong with this game, wait for it to be on sale first of all before buying for the best worth for your money.

My favorite RTS of all time, if you miss having an RTS that isn't based on hyper speed clicks or over in 5 minutes (starcraft 2 , C&C, warcraft 3, etc.) or based on super hero units with just a couple side units then this is your game.

I must have played this game hundreds of hours, not only the steam-version but also an earlier version.

What is very unique about it, is it's great epic battles. You expand your empire. You build your fleet(s). And when the decisive face-off with your opponent finally has come, "Sins of Solar Empire: Rebellion" gives you the most brilliant epic battles you will ever have seen in RTS.
Don't be mislead by my words. There will be lots of matches, where victory or defeat is inevitable and unspectacular. You won't see much of the "magic" then. 
Of course that all depends on your game settings, strategy and the quality of your opponents. You can set the game to go faster. Then you will experience 30 minute matches in PvP or PvE, that leave little time for micromanagement and decisions. Or you can really go epic and slow, where you carefully make your choices and feel the electricity in the air ... uhm ... void I mean ... , as your fleets slowly close the distance and hell brakes loose. Then you will see how every choice you make affects the battle and finally turns the tide. Also, "rock paper scissors" still applies. With huge fleets and many different ship types, finding the right line-up is not trivial.
You can choose from a wide variety of settings, to get the game to be more of a minimalistic skirmish or almost turn-based. I once left a slow singleplayer match for a few seconds and it turned out to take me 15 minutes. I had forgotten to pause. When I returned, my fleet had fought off some space pirates but nothing else happened. In other games I might have returned just in time to see the final building of my base collapse. 
Whatever floats your capital ship. If you have played the traditional SOASE, the capital ships there were really big and important for your micromanagement. But now you get the Titan, sort of a huge hero unit unique to every faction. Nothing can survive long in the presence of a Titan and as it "learns" it becomes a fleet in being, crushing entire enemy fleets.

Establishing your empire gets a bit of the old "Master of Orion" feeling. You conquer planets, build up stuff on them and in the orbit.
Orbit is a nice key word. The battles don't take place in space but in the orbit around contested planets. The planets are connected through space lanes. That may narrow down your options and spoil the open-world idea of an RTS game fought in space. On the other hand it creates nice tactical elements like bottle necks or flanking maneuvers.

Another great aspect is diplomacy leading to alliances, which even grant advantages in combat.

Unfortunately the game still has some balancing issues in PvP which is not helped by the fact, that the player community has shrunk and you will encounter lots of veteran players. You might get frustrated. But the game also has a great PvE mode and the AI is not bad at all. Sometimes the AI is rushing into a futile battle. But then again they seem to calculate their odds on-the-fly and retreat even before you know you won, only to be back before you expected them to. For SP I would recommend downloading some maps from the community, cause the PvP maps are all about balance and symmetry and PvE should be more about atmosphere and exploration. There are maps out there with huge star systems, where a game will last for days, mind this is still RTS, not "Civilization". 
With the option to get AI on your side or more on the enemy side, with - I think up to 8 - teams and difficulty settings, everyone can get a challenging yet enjoyable game experience.

You will need to play hundreds of hours to get all of the tactical depth of this title and still be surprised. And if you really think you have seen it all, you can benefit from the community friendliness of SOASE. The community has been very active and there are not only lots of maps and units and "improved balancing" tweaks but also great mods.
I cannot tell which one you will like best as that depends on your nerdiness. However there are two very impressive mods based on the universes of Star Wars and Star Trek and even a Battlestar Galactica Mod, that i have not tried yet.
Other game developers make you pay for every piece of DLC, cutting off fans from implementing their own ideas. Ironclad Games and Stardock stick with another philosophy here. To try your own ideas, the game comes with two tools, a quick map designer and an editor. Thanks for that, by the way, really appreciated. Ironically that makes the game still attractive today and people are still buying it.

Any negative points? Well, the game is from 2012 and graphics might not be thrilling anymore plus you will play zoomed out most of the time and not see much of it anyway. I have it run smoothly on medium settings even on my old Core2 notebook. Also, if you prefer fast paced RTS with a focus on gut feeling and micro managing small troops, then you might be more comfortable with "Company of Heroes" or something similar. Personally, I like both, but they are very different. I would never start a game of SOASE if i knew, I only have got an hour of time. In Singleplayer you can pause and even accelerate but it will never be a casual play.
Another flaw is that units may take the initiative if not carefully set. Sometimes a ship will come back to the fight although you ordered it away and be destroyed because of some older stance. You can merge ships to different fleets or release them, but every now and then they do what they want. When you command hundreds of ships, that is not what you need. Also sometimes you will have trouble noticing a minor push or incident because the interface is not that well arranged.

So all in all I would highly recommend SOASE:R to anyone looking for a unique RTS experience in a scifi world. The game, at present, is still worth its 75% discount, largely due to the open design and mods. I would not pay more, since it's an older title. If you are not sure, you can wait for a further drop or a bundle.

You can choose between 3 Races: TEC (Trader Emergency Coalition) they are human, The Advent was originally a desert religious cult that mastered psychic powers and The Vasari they are the only alien race in the game. A new feature: For every race (TEC,Advent,Vasari) you can choose between Loyalists and Rebels both of them have their own advantages and abilities. This version of the game is the original SOASE game with add-ons (like Titan-class ships).  It seems to be re-balanced so that newbies don't get wiped out, as they did in the final patches of the original game years ago.  Even on the lowest difficulty levels, that last patch made the game unplayable.

This version rolls that back, as long as you're not trying to attack everyone at once and you make good use of pirate raids.  I finished a game a few days ago, maxing out all the tech trees, maxing my fleet, wiping the pirate home world, and wiping out all my rivals.  Note:  wiping out a capital, for some reason, wipes out your enemy with the default options.  In the end of that game, there were 4 or 5 planets left of one of my rivals, but I left them for last since they weren't attacking me directly.  When I wiped out my other remaining rival, the game ended with me winning, even with those planets still in enemy control.

This is a very complicated game at first.  Play all of the tutorials.  Pause the game right at the beginning, and read over the tech tree - ALL OF IT.  Understand that some buildings, like trade ports and media hubs, are gated by the number of labs you've built, and as such, building trade and media advancements is not available immediately, and is not nearly as important as weapons, shields, armor and fleet logistics (you can't build what you can't support).  At the same time, don't max fleet logistics in the beginning, because of increasing recurrent fleet support costs dragging down your income - take some planets, build up their incomes, take as many planets as you can before you can't win battles, THEN raise fleet logistics and defend what you have until you've built enough ships to take more planets.

One important point:  pirates will destroy some of your planets over time.  This should be expected, and you should have a colony ship ready to rebuild such planets the second the pirates clear out of the system (pirates do not colonize planets).  Pirate attacks can keep your enemies at bay, but as the bounty goes higher, they will not only attack your enemies, but you too.  Yes, you will scream at this when it happens, but get used to it.  It's better to spend that money, tie up the enemy, and rebuild a planet than it is to get wiped by your enemies (who will pay the pirates to go after you, too).  Just remember that by the endgame, you will be able to wipe out the pirate home world completely at a time of your choosing, then any remaining pirate swarms.  In the meantime, the pirate swarms are so big that all but the largest fleets will not be able to take out a swarm without losing many ships, and that's during the entire game.  And that's just one swarm - the next cycle's swarm will be bigger...and bigger.  The best way to survive is to get out of the pirates' way, and pound your real enemies who can take your planets, colonize them and use them against you.

The bigger the galaxy, the longer the game will take.  Small and medium, you can probably finish in a day.  Large and higher will take multiple days to play through and win.

If you are running this in 4K, be sure to get in the MAIN MENU settings (i.e., not within a game you're playing) and set the interface scaling to at least 200%, otherwise you will probably be unable to read any of the text.  Thanks to Fyst for showing me (and now you) how to do that.

Main Menu  -->  Options  -->  User Interface  -->Scaling (bottom right)  -->  set to 200% (or to taste).

TL;DR:  It's not Master of Orion 2, but it's a good strategic and tactical game.  If it gets overwhelming, hit the Pause key, and look everything over.  Take your time at first, because there's a learning curve.  Most of all, when you start a new game, your opponents each have a difficulty setting, and IT IS NOT AT THE EASIEST LEVEL.  Click through all the difficulties until you get the one-chevron Easiest level for each enemy, otherwise you may get stomped.  Use the pirates, but don't go toe-to-toe with them.  Up your planet colonization and fleet techs, take planets until you can't, then upgrade fleet capacity.     Wash, rinse, repeat.  Save cultural and trade techs for near the end, because your fleets are your life's blood.

Good luck.

[h1]TL:DR? See Conclusion[/h1]

[h1]INTRODUCTION:[/h1]
Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is a massive real-time strategy game developed by Ironclad Games and published by Stardock Entertainment. It is the third standalone expansion in the popular Sins of a Solar Empire line of games and stands as testament to why this genre can only work with the PC Platform. Although the game is classified as an RTS, it does feature a lot of 4X (Civilization type) elements which the developers are calling the 'RT4X' genre.

[h1]PLOT (No Spoilers):[/h1]
The player takes control of a space faring civilization whose sole objective is to be the most dominant force in the Galaxy. Achieve this either through military force, diplomatic means or economic superiority. Lead your civilization from a small single planet colony into a vast interplanetary empire spanning multiple worlds and multiple star systems.

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
+ Epic in scale (The player can choose to either play in one solar system only, or expand their empire to other solar systems if the map permits)
+ Massive space combat and intense fleet engagements
+ Beautiful Graphics and Visuals
+ Good ship and space station variety
+ Ship and space station customization and upgrades
+ Complex and solid core gameplay
+ Simple and easy to manage Empire Tech Tree
+ Incorporates the features of the previous expansions without forcing you to buy them
+ High replayability
+ Seamless Zoom Function (Marvel at your fleet or the intense ship on ship combat)
+ Playable even with some lower end computers
+ Modding potential (Example: See Star Trek 3 Armada mod)

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
- No Campaign mode and even if there was...(see below)
- Story is negligible
- Steep learning curve
- Capital/Titan Ships and Space stations have no hardpoints (see Star Wars: Empire at War space combat)
- Only three main factions to play (although there are 6 sub-factions)
- Stardock Account Management

[h1]CONCLUSION:[/h1]
GREAT GAME but NOT FOR EVERYONE. If you're the type of gamer who's really into real-time strategy or 4X games and have a lot of free time to burn, then this game would be great.

[h1]WORTH IT?:[/h1]
GOOD BUY and HIGHLY RECOMMENDED for Space, Sci-Fi, RTS and 4X fans.

[h1]FINAL NOTES:[/h1]
It's massive in scale with dozens of ships clashing in some of the most epic space warfare I have ever seen. Outside of combat, it has a good and complex empire management system akin to the 4X genre. The game also runs surprisingly well with the last generation computer systems since its game engine still only need the system requirements back in 2008 when it was first released.

Epic space strategy at its best! Sins polished game engine allows seamless navigation from the micro managment of your individual planetary systems & military units all the way out to the full solar system view allowing large scale tactical management.

At close range, all galactic elements as well as the ship & stations have very high level of graphic detail; they look fantastic! When you zoom out this detail is replaced with a clear tactical overlay making it easy to transition between tasks, all intuitively done with the mouse scroll wheel & pointer location. UI is low frills, but very functional.

A.I. is also well designed, smart & strong! If you are not quick & know your strategy, at harder difficulties, they will give you a real battle for your survival! Further challenges can be found in the achievements, which challenge you to only research one tech tree or not to build a type of ship. These mix up the gameplay & I enjoyed trying to get these ones. I'm still hunting for the elusive [b]Space Ponies![/b] :)

DLCs so far have been relatively small feature enhancements, but all worthwhile grabbing as they add a few more new things to the Sins universe. There are also some great total conversion mods (& other mods) out there to try, like one of my favs, the Star Wars total conversion mod called [url=http://www.moddb.com/mods/sins-of-a-galactic-empire][u]Sins of a Galactic Empire[/u][/url]. Worth checking out.

Sins pretty much has it all from unique alien factions, diplomacy & extensive tech trees to missions & trading. Also population, battle & resource management & massive planetary sieges involving hundreds of ships.

The shear scale means games can go for days! Epic game!

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is one of the most versatile space based RTS games produced; the vanilla game offers three distinct factions and each of those has a sub faction you can choose; loyalist or rebels, each with different tech and construction options. The research trees are fairly comprehensive and cover everything from civilian, military, diplomatic and defence branches each with 30-40 techs in each branch. Therefore there can be different strategies each playthrough to some extent. But the combat is fairly satisfying as well as visually pleasing but the real beauty of Sins is the vast repository of mods available for it on sites like ModDB - Sins of a Galactic Empire (Star Wars), Star Trek Armada 3 are probably two of the most comprehensive you could check out, but there are many more. Therefore as well as the great base game you also have access to whatever particular science fiction genre you want to simulate with the solid game engine. What I would suggest for those familiar with them are programs like large address aware; but more for the mods as opposed to the base game as they tend to crank up the population capacity of ships compared to vanilla. (Due to engine constraints it only utilises the old school 4gb of ram limitation even if you have 16gb; LAA or similar will remedy this problem and allow for late game battles on a massive scale.)

Super long version:

I love Master of Orion II. That is, I love a sci-fi turn based strategy game with infinite replayability. But it's an old game and I'm constantly questing to find something newer that could be its equal. Therefore, it was only natural that I'd find Sins and give it a spin.

Sins isn't turn based - instead it's moving and flowing all the time. Instead of "just one more click" (JOMC?) it keeps you drawn in, hyper aware to act and react in the game and oblivious to the world around you for hours on end. I prefer playing slow but when you play as single player you can easily turn up the speed in-game. You can also set how long it takes to do research, build stuff etc. so you can sort of affect the pace of the game. When I play multiplayer with my friends they like to play FAST so it is a very intense experience with high click rate and Rapid Eye Movement.

I love the different races, factions and their different ships and tech! They distinguish themselves both aestetchically and how they play. Another reason I stuck with Sins was that I was trying to figure it out. In the aforementioned MOO2 there were clearer strategies - for example, what tech should you get first in order to, say, rush your opponent. I was looking to understand these strategies and counter-strategies in Sins and I guess I still am. Playing with my friend has helped a lot since he is much more logical and strategically minded, and also wants to discover the possible strategies.

Recently, I have discovered the modding community for Sins and it is as if a whole new world has opened for me! There are mods for updating the effects and graphics of Sins to make it look a lot better! There are mods to make the different races and factions more different, yet balanced in between themselves. There are mods that bring completely new races, ships and tech trees into the game. There's cool mods for Star trek fans, Star wars fans, Halo fans..the list goes on - don't miss out on the mods!

Some players complain about this game being 32-bit and singlethreaded, but it's been running fine on high settings on my 10 year old LINUX machine, so I don't see the problem. A worse problem IMO is the AI which I think could be a bit smarter..but that's been partially amended by mods.

Everyone keeps wishing for Sins 2 and so do I. But it will be hard to make new game that is better than the old one!

9 years after release, people still play this in almost-thousands.
And who can blame them - the gameplay was and still is a godsend to 4x RTS games.
On the surface, it seems simple - Developing infrastructure on planets is far from a grand startegy type of deal.
Same for fleets - each faction has ships that go pew pew against other ships, some are better at one thing than others per rock-paper-scissors logic. Then you get to think - How to keep your capital ships safe? How to reinforce fleets in time? Do I focus on cruiser firepower, strike craft, capitals? Am I using the most powerful ability of them all here? Is the kinetic arms upgrade worth it over another armor upgrade? Oh look, Advent has found my armada, they come in force... HOLY SHIT, THE BEAMS! ARE YOU SURE IT'S FROM 2012?
Yes, the presentation is one of the game's strongest suits, that faced the many years with pride and dignity; combine it with the scale of the game it can end up and you'll see truly fair scenery.
Also, mods. This game is some of the first ones to have stayed around due to huge modding scene. It's about as stalwart as this game, and features great many total conversions that actually do alter and develop the gameplay blueprint. Halo, Star Wars, Stargate, and more, have mods that will double the game's already great replayability. Multiplayer also exists, and tons of other reviews can divulge you how grand this is.
Conclusion: Another classic 4x, and one of the publisher's finest hours. I give it a very large number of Cobalt class frigates, over their average life expectancy in battle versus Eradica titan.

I reinstalled Beanie Hunter (The Division 2) the other day hoping my initial decision to remove it from my PC was too rash. 5 hours later as my Internet received the last of about 60 gig of install files I decided to reinstall Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. In the time it took my PC to finish dilly-dallying around with Beanie Hunter I had already downloaded, installed and set up a quick skirmish on Sins. One hour later and I totally forgot I had even purchased yet alone just downloaded 60 gig for the second time in one month.

How can one game be so small (about 1gig) and so underrated with such a small budget yet be so much better in every single way. A strange comparison to make I know but it just really hit home how good Sins is when I had just spent another £60 on yet another wet title from Ubisoft and there I was uninstalling it for the second time in one month and reverting to spending time conquering a small corner of the galaxy in Sins. 

Pound for pound there is no game more worthy than Sins. It originally cost me £10 back in 2012 on sale and is about 2gig when installed and it does so much for and with so little! Originally the game had some flaws which held me back from praising it such as the limitations of the game running smoothly during multilayer skirmishes but this was sorted a long time ago and I can honestly say that, other than C&C red alert and COH2 this is just the best RTS you can spend time playing.

The only thing lacking is any kind of story. There is some background lore but on the whole no real story or campaign. The reason it is so good is the simplicity. The only real learning curve is in the research or tech tree but even this is about 75% standardised across each faction with each faction also having some pecific tech available to them. Literally left click, right click your way to galactic domination. 

The game has 3 factions each split into a rebel or alliance sub faction meaning 6 factions in total. Each has unique units and abilities and each start liking or hating other factions diplomatically. You start with one planet and a few scouts and it is up to you to firstly map the system you are in and then commence the domination! From a diplomacy point of view there ain't much there really but that's okay. You can make pacts with other factions and even with space pirates! Or simply convert your riches into a bounty for a faction who is giving you trouble and then sit back and watch a hundred pirate ships go raiding their territory before timing your own invasion. 

Units and weapons are nice, very nice. Each faction has 6 unique capital ships as well as a Titan which is unique to the specific sect you have chosen. You then get about 6 bigger cruisers and 6 smaller frigates as well as tiny fighters and bombers. Zoom all the way out so that your system is all visible on one screen or zoom in and follow a tiny bomber as it makes an attack run on an enemy. All the above for 2gig. There are loads of different planets which can either be colonised straight away or after research, there are defenses, planetary shields, superweapons, wormholes and basically every thing you could need for a sci-fi RTS romp around the galaxy. 

Final words, buy this game. Just buy it. If you have friends who enjoy RTS then buy a copy for them too as it is just excellent to play over the Internet or LAN, yeah that's right remember when games built in a LAN infrastructure for those of us old enough to remember playing multi player in the same room as the other players! The way the game displays your empire on screen is a revolution. So many units and planets under your control by the end would normally make for a cluttered and complicated display but they have pulled it off in epic fashion. For the best ever non complicated space RTS look no further.

A truly wonderful space based RTS. The 3 races play very differently from one another and the sub-factions are distinct enough to make you change your style depending on whether you're the Loyalists or Rebels.

The game's pace can be easily adjusted in the pregame options to suit your skill and the AI does a good job of building counters to your units (e.g. you build long range, AI builds corvettes). Having said that, the AI has a greater emphasis on the Artifical as opposed to Intelligence as it essentially attempts to win through attrition.

But such AI strategies are to be expected and, in my opinion, lead to some pretty epic battles. Build a starbase on a key chokepoint and station a fleet there to try and hold the line, if you're playing Hard or higher the AI will be charging your line in no time with capital ships, frigates, corvettes, cruisers and even titans.

The game is also extremely moddable. If you can read this review you can mod a good portion of Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. There are also tonnes of mods already created (Halo, Star Wars, Star Trek, etc.).

Finally, while the game does not have a campaign I personally feel this is no loss. Honestly ask yourself, "Would I play the campaign more than three times?" Probably not unless there was some meaningful reward (which would be difficult to work into the game). As a result, the omission of a four to eight hour campaign is no big loss.

I could go on and on but I'm worried you'll keep reading when you should just go get the game already!

The last time I wrote a review it was for a LEGO game. This couldn't be more different--in plenty of good ways.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is one of those games you can pick up without any experience with its predecessors in the franchise--or without any experience with other RTS games, like me--and still have a fun time with it. The non-turn based gameplay makes for fun, action-packed, immersive experiences, and the sheer level of detail in both the visuals and the game mechanics are to be admired. The three factions, which are then broken into two sub-factions each, are all unique in special, and usually deadly, ways that allow for a variety of different ways to play.

The game features both single player and multiplayer modes, both of which can be customized to fit the player(s). The AI that can be added to a game can be adjusted in difficulty however one pleases, as can the map size and types of planets. There's even a map customizer that allows you to build your own star system or systems with a few clicks on some drop-down menus, and then explore them while battling off enemy fleets and the occasional marauding pirates.

The DLC for this game is also definitely worth investing in, and I don't say that about a lot of games; with all three main DLC packs you get more varieties of planets and other cosmic bodies, more planetary upgrades, more research categories, new maps, and the option to have more frequent and more deadly enemies such as pirates and rebel factions, all of which further enhances the game. However, I'd still advise waiting for a sale and buying it all together for sometimes up to half the price, because as fun as it is to conquer a galaxy, sometimes you still wanna do it on a budget.

I've owned this game for a few years now, and not once has it disappointed me. This is the one RTS game I recommend to almost everyone I know that even remotely have an interest in gaming. And now I'll happily recommend this game to you, too. Enjoy your galactic conquest.

First Review Ever

[h1] The Great [/h1]
[list]
[*] Breath Taking [url=http://i.imgur.com/1eRuaB6.jpg] Visuals [/url]
[*] The term from the first game "Unrivaled Scale", they aren't joking, I've had games against the AI with friends last as long as 12 hours. (You can save and come back later)
[*] Introduction of Subfactions to each species doubles the faction options from 3 to 6.
[*] Includes everything from previous Sins games.
[*] As a Former Halo Player, I have high extremely high standards to what a soundtrack should be like. Bought the soundtrack, best decision I've ever made [url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iI8aCw5eEh0] TEC Loyalists - Watching The Borders [/url] Absolutely beautiful soundtrack. Unique to each faction, and deviations for each subfaction.
[*] Surprising amount of depth, you've got your defense to manage, your own fleet for attacking targets, resource generation to worry about, politics and diplomacy are surprisingly in depth if you do some reading about how the game works. UPGRADES FOR EVERYTHING JUST LISTED TO CONSIDER. Yes, you can upgrade your diplomacy, something our current world could bother doing.
[*] If the person hosting has the DLC for the game, everyone gets access to it. Forbidden Worlds adds new types of planets, if the host has it, you'll see these planets in game and you can get the research for them, colonize them etc. Also applies to Stellar Phenomena, if the host has it, you'll get stuff like Coronal Mass Ejections screwing with your planets, but then the'll move on else where (maybe to your enemy). Just like Random Crits in TF2: They Give and Take.
[*] ALL SHALL FEAR YOUR SUBFACTION SPECIFIC TITAN AND FACTION SUPER WEAPON AND YOUR FLEET OF MIGHTY CAPITAL SHIPS
[/list]

[h1] The Good [/h1]
[list]
[*] You can change victory conditions and in game speed of progression, this game takes awhile to play.
[*] Multiple types of victory conditions like "Capital" means you actually have an objective that isn't going to take 10 hours to complete if you don't set them, else it defaults to "Last Man Standing" which means you have to completely clean out your enemies. I recommend playing Capital Victory first time around.
[*] If you want to sit down and conquer a galaxy, you can, but it's gonna take awhile (~4 - 6 hours based on opponent)
[*] If you want to conquer [u] Multiple Galaxies [/u] you can, but it's gonna take awhile. (8+ hours based on opponent)
[*] If you want to fight over a single star system with just a handful of planets, you can! (2 - 4 hours based on opponent)
[*] Surprisingly simple interface that noobies can use easily, and vets can master with a bit of poking around.
[/list]

[h1] The Bad [/h1]
[list]
[*] As said before, depending on your scenario, this game can take AWHILE to play. Depends on your view, but I've gotta throw this in The Bad section because spending half your day conquering a Galaxy is both kickass and tedious at the same time.
[*] Besides capital ships, most of the Frigates and Cruisers don't seem to have much strategy behind them except "Build a bunch of everything". More Experianced players will know how to use these, but it's not immediately clear to noobies the difference between each of the frigates. Cruisers doesn't have this apply as much to them, but it's still worth noting.
[*] Frustratingly slow start up to each game. You'll be scraping the bottom of the barrel for resources and unlike other games that don't allow you to manage resources, you simply get continous deposits, you'll find yourself never getting a head.
[*] Fighting online you will either run into people that don't have enough time to sit down and enjoy a game, not really the game's fault, but it's worth noting. OR they'll be so damn good you don't even stand a chance. I typically play Free For All with optional alliances, so you can build up with other factions that might be on your door step, and plot against those that'll be gunning for you. Alliances with other factions with their own alliances do not carry over to you, so you can absolutely obliterate your ally's allies.
[/list]

[h1] The Ugly [/h1]
[list]
[*] Very difficult for noobie players, or even people that know what their doing but haven't played in awhile, to... hate this word, MICROMANAGE [u] everything. [/u]  You've got so much you're going to have to put your attention on. Planetary defense is probably the biggest issue under the Micromanagement department. The Vasari have a ship that can be told to "Autoplace" mines. Something similar for planetary defense. I wish part of a planet's income was also stored as "defense" budget so you could place defenses around one planet without drawing out of your own resources. Because you're going to be scraping the bottom of the barrel just playing the game as is. Late game when you have all the money you could possibly imagine, it stops being a resource issue and becomes a management issue. Because you've gotta do it all manually. If it applied individually per planet, and each planet had it's own defense budget that built up over time, pulling out a defense would be a lot more feasible for EVERY planet in your domain. I suppose this is to make it so you don't turtle on every planet, and you need to concentrate your resources to defending the key points, like the planets you own that are next to enemy planets, or defending wormholes, the centre star, etc. It feels like you should be able to defend every planet equally simply because the options are there. But if you're fighting the AI, the AI is WAY better at Microing than any human player, and you WILL find defenses on every planet, and that's why this is so frustrating.
[/list]

[h1] On The Fence [/h1]
[list]
[*] You'll control the battles by specifically saying which targets to attack, and with what, when to use abilities so on. But this hinges on whether or not you have something that can counter what the enemy is throwing at you. The only solution to fighting a Titan is either a fleet of capital ships or another Titan. Throwing the lesser ships (Frigates and Cruisers) at the larger ships (Capital Ships and Titans) is basically useless. This is entirely for balance issues. If you could build a bunch of crappy frigates and beat a captial ship, there'd by no point to building capital ships.
[*] The biggest thing you'll control in a battle is when to retreat. Not bad, not good, this is stuff that's on the fence. There is depth to the battles, but once again this comes down to that word again... MICROMANAGEMENT. You can just Macro (I.E CTRL + A, and then attack) instead of Micro, but the best results come from Micro... once again, not bad, not good, this stuff is on the fence.
[/list]

[h1] Notes [/h1]

It may look like this game has a lot of "bad" being shipped with it. It's really because there's SO MUCH to do, there is SO MUCH DEPTH to the game that this is really the best system that could go along with it. Note that I never offered points of improvement except to defence, because there isn't much that can be done to improve the series. The series has evolved from just "Sins of a Solar Empire" through multiple expansions like... entrenchment, diplomacy, which has added more (and for the better) to the game. The realty is, you are one person, and you can't run an empire with just one person... and that's the biggest strength and flaw to the game. You are one person that can manage an interstellar empire, the devs have done their absolute best work to make sure you can MANAGE your empire, but there is just SO MUCH to do...

And that's why I love this game. Really, you could call "Sins of a Solar Empire" Galactic Empire Management Simulator, one that is rather serious, but a Simulator regardless. Because you'll be managing every aspect you can imagine.

First review in a while, but this game deserves it.

I'll start out with the somewhat common "my playtime is inaccurate" speech, having played more than 200 hours of this and it's previous incarnations through Impulse.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is truly one of a kind. This version basically combines the entirety of the 2 previous titles, Trinity and regular ol' SoaSE, so Rebellion truly has it all and more.

As such, this review is kind of both a Rebellion review and SoaSE in general review, because I've never reviewed the original or Trinity as there is no real story to this game, which makes it a difficult game to even explain to the masses who enjoy story driven games.

I tend to play a Single Player skirmish with 2 or 3 Hard AI players, however in the past have spent a great deal of time playing lengthy LAN matches, which were loads of fun, but ultimately one of the only major flaws of SoaSE comes out through such lengthy matches, even just playing against AI.
That flaw has been given a bad wrap in more recent times because of the evolution and adoption of Multi Core processor technology.

Essentially this game does not utilise multicore CPU's and unfortunately there is no fix for this, even after extensive research and optimisation mod trialling. But to their credit, those mods are great for getting the game to run on lower spec systems, laptops, virtualisation/steaming etc, but no mod can add 64bit or multicore support. That's the game's engine limitation, and it's not the only one around... I'm looking at you Cities XL.

It is important to note that at regular playing speed, this takes tens of hours of a single match to even be a problem, but on lower spec, lower (and older) GHz systems, this happens within about an hour give or take 30mins of regular speed play time with a couple of AI players.

With all that said, one of THE greatest longevity features for me is the ability to speed up the game time by 2x, 4x and 8x increments, even in a LAN match (host must change it).

Because of the vast expanses of space and [travelling] time at regular speed, this speed up feature can actually make for a much more challenging game, albeit much faster. Generally you will have to sacrifice micro management for macro at those speeds, but on large scale maps with only 2 or 3 players, with multiple star systems, the ability to speed up hyperspace travel from a distant planet to another is a HUGE time saving and action creating element and there is no penalty or lock down on the control of the game speed that you have, apart from it's 4 presets, so interchanging between them can be as fluid as zooming in or out and the speed controls can be remapped as well as basically everything else.

When I first discovered this speed up feature in the original Sins, it was, at first, not something I was looking for or really cared about, largely because I was still learning the controls and the game at the time.
When I was finally bored with the amount of time it took to setup, capture, defend, build and deploy, it would be too long for a single game session, and that bothered and still bothers me.

Command & Conquer (up until and including 3) had the right recipe for possible lengths of a single player skirmish battle. With Sins this isn't possible at regular speed, that is if you're interested in actually establishing a large empire of any sort instead of rushing with a dozen weak ships, which gets stale fast. 

The camera controls in Sins are very fluid and quite unique, and once you get the hang of it, there really is nothing like it, some things are similar but the ability to orbit and zoom freely around any axis while fixed on a certain point is impressive, and the instant ability to track any of your fleet and zoom right in to the ship and it's details or zoom right out to galaxy level all in real time and fluid as your mouse can move. An RTS camera/movement system that IMO rivals that of what Blizzard, Westwood or EA have ever done is definitely worth a mention in this review.

The 3 original factions, the TEC, Advent and Vasari have been Loyalist-ised and given their Rebel counterparts in this final Sins title and have created many new ways of playing the game. I found that this is by far the most balanced of the 3 in the series mainly because of the 3 extra sub-faction additions, which also open up Role-Playing type elements of having say, 3 Rebel factions vs 3 Loyalist factions in a desperate struggle to take control over a strange galaxy.

The in-game Map Designer is also worth a mention, although it takes a fair bit of trial and error to get something you're happy with, and even then playing your own creations can sometimes backfire or surprise you in ways you never thought possible.
The only downside is the lack of manipulation you have on Planets and Stars. The "Map Designer" is basically a Map Generator.
If you've ever wanted to take on several hundred space pirate homeworlds in the one solar system then Sins is for you!
But in all seriousness, the Map Designer does a pretty good job once you learn how it works and ways you can create interesting maps just by changing sliders and numbers.
If you're really serious about designing your own Solar System or Galaxy then Ironclad have supplied everyone with their GalaxyForge editor which is used to create the many included Single and Multiplayer premade maps. 

My Pros & Cons shortlist;

Pros:
+ One of a kind space-based RTS gameplay
+ Useful and informative dialogue boxes, hovering over icons has been given great attention to detail.
+ Massive tech tree
+ Awesome scale of real time space battles and large scale empire building.
+ Fine control over placement of your buildings, or for riskier, faster matches, an "Auto place" feature for Buildings which is also a +
+ Interesting and unique items, ships, power-ups, upgrades
+ The graphics scale really well across many many different types of systems, but the close up details can be a bit disappointing even at Ultra settings.
+ Inclusion of both a Map Designer & GalaxyForge editor.

Cons:
- Fairly steep learning curve and long match times
- Units (mainly Capital Ships) of the same type have to be upgraded individually, on a small scale this is less important then on a larger one.
- No minimap
- Left Planet, Structure and Unit tree can't be hidden. Capturing more than 10-20 planets adds much more time navigating and cuts any efficiency of the tree at all.
- Some tasks would be better left automated, such as the 2 scout ships that you start with should have their exploration ability Autocast set to on, not off. Also Metal and Crystal mines could be auto-built after you have captured a planet and have the resources to spare
- At regular speed it takes far too long to reach higher tech levels in a single match
- Can be boring in stages of early travel or exploration. Once you've seen the same variations of desert, ice, volcanic, terran and asteroids over and over, the excitement wears down over time (tens to hundreds of hours for me)
- Not just a con of Sins, but most RTS games really need the ability to 'mute' a certain Unit or Building you are queuing up and and creating 50 or 100+ of the same Units and the game wants to announce the successful creation of every single one.

The following describes my experience every time I play this game.

The first scenario.

I take my sweet time, playing turtly and expanding slowly, mainly because I'm still fresh from Endless Space and rapid expansion is dangerous, in my mind. I fully upgrade every single world until I can make my empire like a house, except I paint each indavidual brick before I lay it, polish it, and make it amazing. A slow process.

Then the enemy fleet arrives, bristling with LRM frigates and siege engines, capitol ships all over the damn place, shredding my meager defenses while I scramble to make some kind of response fleet. I lose in minutes when this happens. Hours of work, gone in seconds.

The second scenario.

I make one capitol ship right off, usually the one with colonization capability, and build a fleet to defend it before I even start growing. From there, I expand. The colonization fleet dives into the universe and takes everything not bolted down, planting my flag in every piece of dirt they can find. While this is happening, I'm researching like a madman. Everything from the civilian tree goes first, mainly mining and expansion assistance. I'm able to colonize any world by about minute fifteen, and do so with abandon.

While the colonization fleet is away, I build up the battle fleet. More capitol ships, hundreds of frigates and cruisers, and a Titan being build in the corner of my home gravity well. My scouts find pirates, enemy players/AI, and all number of worlds. I take everything I can get my hands on and build up more gauss cannons than I can count. If anyone pokes around my systems, they don't leave alive.

Finally, I run into worlds that I can't take with my small colonization fleet. So I pull them back. The enemy mounts an assault, thinking me weak. I let them come, break their backs on my frontier worlds, cracking their armor on my defenses.

Then the battle fleet arrives.

I destroy their assault force in moments, my capitol ships shredding anything in their path, Titan mysteriously AWOL, and drive them back four systems or more before they manage to scramble up a defense. When they do, my Titan and its auxilery fleet arrive...behind them. On a world where they have few defenders, she enters the fray, and ignores the first three worlds completely. Her goal is the capitol. In a desperate attempt to keep their forces strong enough to fight me, the enemy pulls everyone back to the capitol system, and mounts their last stand.

I leave no survivors.



This game is amazing. A little slow, as it usually takes me an hour just to get comfortable with my standing, but oh so very addicting. The above situations happen often, rather than once or twice in a while, and though it does take a long time to build up your fleet, seeing it warp in out of nowhere is a warming experience I've yet to feel elsewhere. Endless space scratched the itch to rule an empire. This scratched my itch to conquer the galaxy.

Space Strategy enthusiasts rejoice: real-time strategy meets 4X rules in a seamlessly zoomable universe that hasn't looked or felt this polished since the original Homeworld game. Marketed as a stand-alone expansion for Sins of a Solar Empire, Rebellion basically sums up every mechanic introduced in every expansion to date - fight off pirates and opposing empires, establish trade routes, colonize or raise every planet in your solar system... and beyond. It has the same addictiveness as Civilization, in that you feel like you're playing a board game in which your faction fights to rule the universe using various tools or domination and manipulation, every match a new iteration in the array of destinies you can forge. On top of that, the space battles are impressive in both scale and effects: tons of freaking laser beams, rockets and machine gun fire keep you at the edge of your seat when a few hundred ships in your fleet meet a few hundred of your opponents' craft and clash in a display of fireworks that is so visceral and pretty it blows your brains out and leaves you slack jawed at the display of awesomeness.

BUY it if you:
-Enjoy RTS games and civ builders alike.
-Want to engage in large-scale space battles with budget hardware (the game's zoom function works like a miracle, letting you join in on epic skirmishes or zoom out to manage your home planet in the blink of an eye).

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is a space strategy game and a real-time strategy (RTS) game which incorporates 4X strategy game elements. This game was developed by Ironclad Games and published by Stardock Entertainment and is only available on PC.

While you may notice another game with Sins of a Solar Empire in its title (Sins of a Solar Empire: Trinity), that is an older version of the game. Rebellion is the definitive and superior version as it not only offers numerous additions to the game, like Titans and new Factions to play as, but also contains everything from the previous versions of the game.

Sins of a Solar Empire does not have a campaign (although it does contain lore and backstory hidden in the game that you can discover through ways such as research and ship descriptions), but instead chooses to focus almost exclusively on gameplay. This is where Sins really shines. Gameplay in Sins takes place in real-time, allowing you to build ships and send them out all the while earning credits through taxing planets and earn metal and crystal through the ownership of asteroids. Sins also implements elements of 4X strategy games into its gameplay. You are able to build structures such as Trade Ports to generate more Credit Income and Research Labs to allow you to research and develop new ships to produce, unlock planets for you to colonize, and upgrade you ships, planets, and structures. All this and more brings more depth and customizability to the strategy of this game that you won’t find in other RTS games. It has been described by its developers as a “RT4X” and that’s a pretty accurate description, in my opinion.

In Sins of a Solar Empire you can build ships which are specialized for different roles such as: Scouting, Colonizing, Deploy Star-Bases (massive upgradable defensive structures), Build and Dock Strike-Craft, Lay Mines, and much, much more. There are Capital Ships which are strong commanding vessels that have various abilities that can be used in battle. There are also a variety of offensive ships that can range from the light frigates and long-range frigates to heavy cruisers and, with Rebellion, small and fast corvettes.

Sins of a Solar Empire was made in 2008 with the original “Iron Engine”. This engine allows the game to render and support in real-time a large number of planets, structures, and hundreds of ships. 

The Iron Engine has not held up as well over time, however. Due to the age of the engine SoaSE was made in, this game will struggle to run after about 2 hours of continuous gameplay with a large number of ships. Late-game lag is unavoidable once you reach about a 2 hour playtime. 

Any more than an extended 2 hours of play and the game can be susceptible to crashes, mini-dumps, and occasionally desyncs. This does not always happen; some games can run 3+ hours without experiencing any of these. But for larger games with 6-10 players, there remains a higher chance of a player dropping before you reach 3 hours. It goes without saying that the longer your game lasts, the scale of the map, and the number of ships, the higher the chance for a crash or mini-dump. While this can be a probable occurrence in game that takes many hours and are of a large scale, this is not something that should often happen to you, as games usually take around 1-2 hours. But it bears mentioning if you plan on playing 10 player maps with 80+ planets for more than 2 hours. Note: Those with high ping may lag the game more or have a higher chance of disconnecting from the server.

While this game does not have a campaign, it can be played in Single Player, as well as Multiplayer, via the option to include computer controlled bots or ai (artificial intelligence). The maps range from pre-set to randomly generated and games can range from 2 players to up to 10 players at once in maps that can contain as few as 20 planets in one single-star system, to over 100 planets in a 10 star system.

The quality of the Ironclad Online (ICO) Server is generally good, although it will occasionally be pulled down for maintenance. This usually only last about an hour or so. The online community for this game is of an average size; about 30-100 players depending on the day; there are regulars who play almost every day and can usually be found in games throughout the week. You will rarely find yourself alone with no one else online, though, depending on your time zone, you may only see one or two players online and only a few games in progress. It can take anywhere from 10 minutes to 1 or 2 hours to fill a room depending on the size and goal of the room. You can find rooms ranging from Free For Alls (FFAs), 2v2s, 3v3s (Called 3s), 4v4s (4s), and 5v5s (5s). You can also find “Comp Stomps” which are rooms where players will fight against the ai. Game length varies, but is usually between 30 minutes to 2 and a half hours.

The 5s, 4s, and 3s, communities are often populated by regulars and skilled players and are sometimes unfriendly to newcomers. If you are new to the game, it is recommended to played in smaller game such as 2v2s, FFAs, Comp Stomps, and occasionally 3v3s until you have some games under your belt. You can also play with your friends and enjoy private matches with them, either versus each other or against bots.

While this game won’t be for everyone, as different gamers like different things in their strategy games, I would recommend this game to almost anyone. If the lack of a campaign and the chance of occasional trouble with Multiplayer aren’t deal-breakers for you, I would highly, highly recommend this game to everyone who likes strategy games. There is truly no other game like it that bridges the gap between RTS and 4X like this game does. You are bound for hundreds of hours of addictive gameplay with Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion! 

EDIT: I forgot to mention this originally: This game has numerous Mods that can offer lots of enjoyment. There are multiple Mods for Star Trek and Star Wars. There are Mass Effect, Stargate, Halo, and Battlestar Galactica Mods. There are even Mods for just the main game with an Enhanced 4X Mod, the Maelstrom Mod, and more. Most of these Mods are also still being updated and whenever Sins itself gets an update, the Mods usually get updated shortly after so they will work with whatever the current version is.

Whether you choose to try out this game or not, I hope this review has been helpful. And if you do choose to buy this game, I hope you enjoy it as much as I do!

Sins of a Solar Empire is technically a real time strategy game with space opera elements, but the pacing of games is slow enough that it feels like a turned based game. To me, this is a good thing.

First, all the other elements aside from gameplay are either fine or good. Music is fine, the space ships look cool, there are some cool and flashy effects, and scale is particularly well done (some fighter class ships give you a sense of scale when compared to the capital ships, or star bases). Animations of the large ships feel slow and weighty, explosions can feel massive, and you can zoom all the way out for a great strategic view or zoom in for a close up look at the action. It all works well enough, though it doesn't quite compete with games like total war.

Gameplay wise, there is a really intricate and interesting set of systems here. You do research, colonize planets, and engage in space battles and diplomacy. There are neutral units guarding planets, so you start by colonizing small asteroids but then ramp up your military to take on earth like planets, and then of course the enemy empires. There are 3 races that all play very different, and each race has two sub factions that change some more minor things. As already mentioned, the pacing of games is really slow: ships take a long time to get anywhere, they maneuver very slowly so there is no real point in much micro managing, research takes a while, resource gathering is fairly slow too, so you find yourself often making a few decisions, then waiting to have enough resources to do something else. For me personally, this is ideal. I hate the twitchy, instant decision making of many RTS (in a lot of other strategy games clicks per minute is often a useful metric... not here). Games last usually at least an hour or more, and depending on the settings, up to ten or more. This game is at the intersection of Age of Empires and Civ.

That said, I do feel like there is a bit missing. There is no campaign. Some critical concepts, like shield mitigation, are not explained. Some mechanics, like culture, don't feel fleshed out and end up being just mostly annoying. In terms of nitpicks, I have quite a few, but in the end they don't detract much from the overall experience.

Bottom line, if you like grand strategy games, space operas, or real time strategy games, you will find something to like and should check it out.

There are a lot of things I love about Sins of a Solar Empire that I feel other RTS don't manage as well. When you're setting up a game there is a massive amount of options to choose from in terms of customisation, you can play in tiny solar systems or massive multi-star galaxies, different special victory conditions such as Home Planet Capture, Flagship Destruction, and some interesting ones such as Culture victory. Semi-neutral pirate factions can be placed in game that can be bought out with bounties, you can choose which AI factions you'll be facing, their difficulty, and how many. The game allows for a maximum of 10 player factions at once each being able to field a massive amount of units, and the limit on the size of the star system(s) in the game is entirely arbitrary, you can even design your own systems with a map maker, the sense of scale in this game is amazing and I've had battles that made me feel like I was re-enacting the Battle of Coruscant from Star Wars III.

The balance between the 3 factions (6 including subfaction choice) in this game while not perfect is very good, it's also one of the more nonlinear interfaction designs I've seen in an RTS and all of the factions feel very unique to one and other with highly differing playstyles and strengths. The balance between macro and micro in this game is superb and I consider it among the best in all RTS. A major issue I've had with RTS like Supreme Commander is to be competitive in online multiplayer requires learning very precise build orders and the placement of every stone on every map so you can extract them for resources quickly. In Sins the macro gameplay will mostly come to important decisions you make such as what tech tree paths to take and when to take them, where and what to spend money on, are you going to buy out the pirates before another faction pays to attack you or risk ignoring them to save money. This game is one of the most open ended and creative RTS I have ever played. You can opt for many creative strategies such as turtling and defending your planets while you let your culture slowly replace enemy planets own culture, you can play as the friendly diplomat trying to forge trade deals with everyone then after becoming an economic power play both sides against the middle by choosing what warring factions to financially support for your own benefit. There are even factions that can choose to roam the galaxy in warfleets that consume planets for resources as they go along while never owning any themselves, I'm really only touching the tip of the icerberg here, the potential for creativity and roleplay in your strategies with this game is endless.

The micro side of the gameplay in this game is great too, each faction has Captial Ships, Titan Ships, and constructable starbases with many abilities to use, movement of your fleet ships and use of their abilities is important, the game has different ship types which each faction has that have their own strengths and weaknesses, making for a sort of more complicated version of Rock-Paper-Scissors. You'll need to scout ahead and keep up to date on what your enemies are doing to know what kind of ships they are building if you want to counter them effectively, and the opposing side will do the same, making for an aggressive loop where you're always trying to counter what the enemy will do next while also trying to come up with a strategy that will let you win and come out on top, whilst you also have to consider other worries during fleet combat such as how your economy will compare to enemies in the future and if they are building superweapons in their backline planets to target you, etc.

There are 6 AI difficulties in this game, Easy, Normal, and Hard being the first 3. Most players will still find Hard challenging even after many hours in this game, the upper 3 difficulties beyond hard are very difficult, your decision making skills, micro gameplay and speed will be pushed to it's limits against the hardest AI even as a Veteran player unless you relate to AI cheese strategies or pitting yourself against a faction or on a map in your favour, yet it is entirely possible to beat the hardest AI in this game with skill alone. Even if you were to only play against AI in this game you could never run out of fun or challenge, the game has a small but active multiplayer scene too that remains active even after all these years.

Highly recommend this game if you like RTS, best I've ever played.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is a 4X real-time strategy from Stardock Entertainment, the few of its kind. This game is a standalone expansion of the previous game Sins of a Solar Empire: Trinity.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion gameplay is exactly the same as the previous game but expanded in some ways. Each faction in Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion has been splitted into two, a loyalist faction and a rebel faction, each with their own unique background story and traits. Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion also introduce new mighty unit called Titan. Titan is unique with each faction. There is also smaller new ship, the corvette unit which is also unique with each faction. This add new elements of strategy and gameplay to the game. Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion also offer two new DLC, one of them contains new feature, the random events, which will affect your gameplay much.

Graphics of Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion has also been improved. Weapons effect, ships boosters and many other space environment graphics are all enhanced, making the big space battles even more epic than ever. Ships and planets also have better texture now. The game still runs optimized despite all enhanced graphics but still unable to utilize more than 2GB of RAM. When the game run out of memory, most of the time it will crash, but it rarely happen unless you're using 3rd party modification.

There are some mods that making Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion even more fun and interesting, like the Star Trek Armada, changing the whole game universe into Star Trek Universe, Federations, Klingons and all.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion is great standalone expansion pack. Great addition to Sins of a Solar Empire fans. I recommend this.

This game is the apex of the old-school RTS genre, despite its flaws. It's scale is still unmatched by any other strategy game out there and while it's not the best platform for modding (due to all sorts of problems with 32 bit games and RAM limits) it still managed to be the basis of a huge number of awesome mods that are better than most games, including Star Trek Armada III (which is massively better either of the other games in the series!) The only thing that hasn't aged well is the controls, though I still like them. Protip: Use middle mouse to rotate and the scroll wheel to zoom in and out while treating the planets themselves like view anchor points, it works better than traditional panning controls do in this game.

One thing I do want to point out: do not go into this expecting Stellaris. This is NOT a grand strategy game AT ALL. Sins of a Solar Empire is the bastard stepchild of Warcraft III and Supreme Commander while being better than both of those games. It is a straightforward mid-2000's to mid-2010s RTS set on a scale that is ludicrous by the standards of that era, but diplomacy is not a focus of this game. This is a game where you build ships and stations and use them to crush your opponents, and while the Advent definitely seem like they are meant to do diplomacy things, it plays out more like a control deck in a card game. You build things that stop your opponents from being able to attack you or claim your planets.

Don't let that dissuade you though. Sins of a Solar Empire is a classic and can run on a glorified potato. If you haven't played Sins, you need to.

Short answer: There's a good reason I still play this.

Long answer: 
Even after 10 years SoaSE is still one of the best examples of a space 4x game out there, and most notably a real time one as opposed to turn based. This is the most recent variant, and the addition of subfactions and Titans adds a good amount to the game. It's age means it runs reasonably well even on older or less powerful systems (like my own), and still has pretty decent graphics. 

It also does a sense of scale between the ships quite well, if not really the planets/stellar bodies you're fighting over. Being able to scroll right in on a single fighter flying through a battle involving hundreds of ships ranging from small escort frigate to collossal titans larger than starbases is always fun. 

Gameplay is a bit more focused on the tactics and strategy of controlling your fleet over empire building, although there is some depth to be found in resource gathering, planet specialisation and research. On the other hand, it does the combat WELL, with even smaller ships having definite and usually useful roles right up to late game, and Capital Ships and Titans earning experience individually, and slowly unlocking more or improved abilities. Admittedly with a large fleet micromanaging the abilities of multiple lighter ship classes across a fleet of a couple hundred, with a dozen capital ships can be a little intense, but that is what the auto-use function is for, letting you focus on key abilities on your linchpin ships. 

Each of the factions has a rather different playstyle and even the relatively small differences between the 'rebel' and 'loyalist' factions of each race can make a big impact on how your domination of local space will play out, favouring isolationism, diplomacy, economic might, strong defenses, aggression, spreading of culture or various other strategies. Each race's fleet also has strengths and weaknesses to be considered. 

This is without even going into the existence of a lot of quality mods with dedicated teams building on the base game adding both original content, factions from well loved sci-fi universes, or outright conversions changing everything up to and including the neutral factions that control star systems before you arrive. Notable ones covered include Star Trek, Stargate, Halo, and SEVERAL excellent Star Wars mods covering multiple eras in the universe. And both the mods and the base game are still receiving support...

If you're a fan of 4x and strategy games, this is an excellent addition to your library. If you're not, the sometimes slow build up until you see large fleets ducking it out in firework show of beams, missiles, lasers and stranger weapons might put you off, but it IS a lot of fun to watch.

DO LIST - buy, play each faction in all its glory, enjoy the music and graphics, slay A.I, play with friends... Then months later download one of the high quality mods that add Star Wars or Halo ships and enjoy all over again. 

PROS- fantastic graphics with reflections of planets and gas clouds glinting off the hules of capital ships, top of the line theme music that fits the moment (I even paid extra for the downloadable music files), race and faction ships are unique and highly detailed, factions are balanced very well allowing for both turtle or aggressive play styles with any faction without having to bend to a specific play styles....but unique enough that they feel different and have interestinf strategy strangths.

CONS- Two things.... The biggest is that when you win or lose a game, it abruptly cuts to a detailed artwork of the outcome, and a screen with all the starts from the game.... Feels very flat and anticlimactic with how much can go into conquering a galaxy (or being annihilated). There needs to be a fantastic cinematic or great explosion to end such a momentous moment. 
#2 it would really expand the SINS universe if there was a langthy single player campaign with more cool cinematics and specific characters to get attached to. I get the feeling there is so much more to the SINS universe and I'm missing out.
It should also add a lot of value and help get more people into the game. 

I guess I can understand why Ironclad hasn't made a replacement for this game. It's still relevant in the space RTS game world and they keep updating it with patches and minor expansion packs.

P.S it would be awesome if there was also a skill tree\ customisable profile that could carry through to each game. Even if it's just unlocking ship skins, lights, special weapons, perks, etc.

Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion continues to stand the test of time as one of the best space real-time-strategy games of its time. Its combination of fleet and faction management, fluctuating economy based on the actions of the player(s), and the various types of AI to battle against as well as varying maps ranging from a a dozen planets to hundreds of planets gives players a range of matches that can last from a few hours to several days, and even up to a week or more. This game can also provide a challenge with its hard and very hard AI that can steamroll you if you are not prepared or provide a casual experience for those who merely want to test different ships or just to get in a quick game.

Pros~
- Ship combat can be very tense and immersive. This is reinforced if, for example, you have a major fleet that is attacking a key planet held by the enemy and then the enemy's main fleet with a titan dropped out of hyperspace. 
- The soundtrack is very calm and adds a feeling of being a space explorer about to make their mark in the cosmos. It is also very adaptive as it changes based on if you are viewing ship combat or just looking at one of your planet.
- While Pirates can be annoying at times, they add a level of danger that will always leave you on your toes as they can attack anywhere and, if you aren't ready, can destroy your undefended colonies and leave a path of destruction in their wake.
- The economy is very fluid and adjust depending on what you buy or sell. If you, for example, sell a bunch of metal, the prices for metal will drop significantly to adjust for the surplus of metal. If you buy a lot of metal, it will raise the price of metal to adjust for the scarcity of it, even though both metal and crystal have a infinite amount, it hurts you if you sell or buy too much.
- Planets have a different amount of resources that changes their value depending on the situation. Planets, for example, that have a large amount of crystal mining or metal mining can help boost the amount of resources to build ships or make upgrades. Planets that are terran or industrial planets or planets that can support a large population will be very valuable as they provide a larger amount of credits than other planets. Some planets can support more logistic slots or more tactical slots, making them desirable for forward bases and choke points.
- The plethora of mods for this game adds even deeper levels of immersion as you can alter the factions and maps to become immersed in your favorite sci-fi universe. Want to lead the Empire in Star Wars to victory with the Executor super star destroyer? Want to bring order to the final frontier and go boldly where no one has gone before? Want to recreate the space battles on Halo? There are mods that are waiting for you to play them.
- Tons of replayability, especially with friends who are willing to change things up and make things interesting.
- Fleshed out research trees for the various factions that can provide powerful bonuses that can help turn the tide of the war with a few unique research options.

Pro and Con~
- Randomized starting points on the map can be an issue as, if you have allies, they can be isolated and quickly taken out of the match. However, they can be a big thorn in your opponents' sides as they can open a separate front and divide your enemies' attention, helping you overrun their planets.
- The voices for various ships is very welcome as it adds a small amount of uniqueness between them as the voice for a frigate will be different from the voice for a capital ship, sometimes. I do wish, however, that they would have taken a page from Star Wars: Empire at War and have voices for when the ships are in combat.

Cons~
- The diplomacy for the AI still needs work and could be fleshed out more as sometimes, the AI will offer bounties that will ask you to attack you allies when they are also your allies. If you and two other AI are all allies with each other, then they should not be offering missions against each other unless their relations with each other have broken down.
 - The main communication voice is the same for all factions. While this is relatively small, it would be better for each faction to have a unique voice that communicates what occurs in the galaxy.

Overall, I would highly recommend this game to anyone who may be interested as it can be very enjoyable, especially with friends, as I have stated earlier. You will rarely find a space game of this magnitude that allows you to control massive fleets in real time and, while they are a few that can compete with SOASE:R, they fall short of this amazing game.
